title: Design and analysis of a MEMS-based bifurcate-shape piezoelectric energy harvester

sections.heading: Design and analysis of a MEMS-based bifurcate-shape piezoelectric energy harvester
sections.text:
Yuan Luo, Ruyi Gan, Shalang Wan, Ruilin Xu, and Hanxing Zhou

Citation: AIP Advances 6, 045319 (2016); doi: 10.1063/1.4948592 View online: http://dx.doi.org/10.1063/1.4948592 View Table of Contents: http://aip.scitation.org/toc/adv/6/4 Published by the American Institute of Physics

sections.heading: Design and analysis of a MEMS-based bifurcate-shape piezoelectric energy harvester
sections.text:
Yuan Luo, Ruyi Gan,a Shalang Wan, Ruilin Xu, and Hanxing Zhou Chongqing Municipal Level Key Laboratory of Photoelectronic Information Sensing and Transmitting Technology, Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications, 400065, Chongqing, Chongqing Municipality, China

(Received 29 December 2015; accepted 19 April 2016; published online 29 April 2016)

This paper presents a novel piezoelectric energy harvester, which is a MEMS-based device. This piezoelectric energy harvester uses a bifurcate-shape. The derivation of the mathematical modeling is based on the Euler-Bernoulli beam theory, and the main mechanical and electrical parameters of this energy harvester are analyzed and simulated. The experiment result shows that the maximum output voltage can achieve $3 . 3 \mathrm { V }$ under an acceleration of $1 \mathrm { g }$ at $2 9 2 . 1 1 \mathrm { H z }$ of frequency, and the output power can be up to $0 . 1 5 5 \mathrm { m W }$ under the load of 0.4MΩ. The power density is calculated as $4 9 6 . 7 9 \mu \mathrm { W } \mathrm { m m } ^ { - 3 }$ . Besides that, it is demonstrated efficiently at output power and voltage and adaptively in practical vibration circumstance. This energy harvester could be used for low-power electronic devices. $^ { © }$ 2016 Author(s). sections.heading: I. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
MEMS-based energy harvesting, otherwise known its system size in millimeters or even smaller, is the process by which ambient energy has gained and converted into electricity to be used in small autonomous devices for making them self-sufficient. The device has an important role in the medical, military, life and many other aspects. Owing of the drawback of the battery, such as its high cost and range ability, this device therefore has been made a great significant attention and research interest for its potential to provide renewable power to replace the traditional power systems, which led by the growing potential application of low-power electronics.1,2

In order to achieve the high voltage and power, the device may be mainly performed with electromagnetic, electrostatic and piezoelectric transducers. Comparing with the other two forms harvester, the piezoelectric transducer has a simpler structure, higher energy density, longer service life, and other advantages. Thus, in recent years, it has developed very rapidl y.16–18 The lower-resonant frequency, output voltage and output power are main performance parameters of this type of device. However the frequency of ambient vibration sources is typically $1 0 0 { \sim } 3 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ .3 Yan $\mathrm { C u i } ^ { 3 }$ presented a new type energy harvester designed for high power at low frequencies, the resonant frequency is $2 6 0 \mathrm { H z }$ while its maximum output power is $1 6 . 7 4 \mathrm { n W }$ when the load resistance is $1 5 \mathrm { K } \Omega$ which is too small for MEMS devices. Farbod Khameneifar4 designed an energy harvester for rotary motion applications with an output voltage of $6 . 4 \mathrm { m V } ,$ it is too big for the microelectronic devices because the volume of the device is $5 0 . 8 \mathrm { m m } \times 3 8 . 1 \mathrm { m m } \times 0 . 1 3 \mathrm { m m }$ .

Based on the above analysis, this work presents a novel piezoelectric energy harvester, which is a MEMS-based device, and this device uses a bifurcate-shape, which could work more efficiently in the low-frequency environment. And this paper is organized as following structures. The theoretical design and analysis model is in Section II which is based on the Euler-Bernoulli beam theory. Simulation results are presented and discussed in Section III. Section IV is the main conclusion.

sections.heading: A. Theoretical design
sections.text: The novel bifurcate-shape energy harvester consists of a main beam and a vice beam. The vice beam has four cantilevers. As the theoretical model shows in Fig. 1. The length, width of main beam is $l , w$ respectively. The length, width of vice beam is $l _ { 1 } , w _ { 1 }$ , respectively. And the length, width of , w,the four cantilevers is $l _ { 2 } , w _ { 2 }$ w, respectively. The device is a symmetrical structure and there is a proof mass at the free end of the cantilever. Considering the beam should have a large elastic modulus and bear a large deformation, the material of the beam is phosphor bronze, the material of piezoelectric layer is PZT-5H, and the material of proof mass is nickel.

sections.heading: B. Analysis of resonance frequency
sections.text:
In order to analyze the feasibility of the structure qualitatively and quantitatively, three degrees of freedom spring-mass model is considered as an equivalent model of the device. According to the literature,5 the quality of the mass is much larger than the rest parts of the device, so the effective mass of the main beam, vice beam and piezoelectric wafer can be neglected. Based on the Euler-Bernoulli beam theory, the resonant frequency $f _ { 0 }$ of the overall system is calculated by the following Eq. (2).5–7

$$
f _ { 0 } = \frac { 1 } { 2 \pi } \sqrt { \frac { k } { m } }
$$

The stiffness coefficient $k$ is given by

$$
k = \frac { 8 E I } { l _ { 2 } }
$$

$$
E I = \sum ( Y _ { i } I _ { i } ) = Y _ { S } I _ { S } + Y _ { P } I _ { P }
$$

Where $Y _ { S }$ and $Y _ { P }$ are the Young’s modulus of the cantilever and the piezoelectric layer, and $E$ is the moment of inertia, $I _ { s }$ and $I _ { p }$ are the area moment of inertia about the neutral axis of the cantilever and the piezoelectric layer, and $m$ is the quality of the mass.

sections.heading: C. Analysis of electrical performance
sections.text:
Based on the piezoelectric constitutive equations and literature,8 while considering the different current produced by different piezoelectric, the current is the charge on the differential of the time,

the total current $i ( t )$ can be written as in Eq. (4).

$$
i \left( t \right) = \sum _ { K = 1 } ^ { N } \left[ \frac { d Q \left( t \right) } { d t } \right] = \sum _ { K = 1 } ^ { N } \left[ - d _ { 3 1 } E _ { P } h _ { p c } \int _ { 0 } ^ { w _ { 2 } } \int _ { 0 } ^ { l _ { 2 } } \frac { \partial ^ { 2 } y _ { r e l } } { \partial x ^ { 2 } } d x - \frac { \varepsilon _ { 3 3 } ^ { s } A } { h _ { p } } \dot { v } _ { p } \left( t \right) \right]
$$

Where $K$ is the number of cantilever, $K { = } 1 , 2 , 3 { \ldots } N , Q ( t )$ is the charge generated in the piezoelectric layer, $y _ { r e l }$ is the displacement which is related to the fixed end of the beam, $E _ { P }$ is the yyoung’s modulus of the piezoelectric layer, $h _ { p c } , h _ { p }$ is the center of piezoelectric layer to the center of beam and the substrate thickness, respectively. $A$ is the area of the piezoelectric wafer, $d _ { 3 1 }$ is the piezoelectric constant of piezoelectric ceramic, and $v _ { p } ( t )$ is the first derivative of the voltage.

vConsidering the Euler-Bernoulli vibration equation, $y _ { r e l }$ can then substitute the separation of variables form given by9–12

$$
y _ { r e l } ( x , t ) = \sum _ { q = 1 } ^ { \infty } w _ { q } ( x ) T _ { q } ( t )
$$

$q$ is the order number of the resonance frequency.

Therefore, the frequency domain of the equation of the total current $i ( t )$ can be obtained by using Fourier transform as follows.

$$
I ( w ) = \sum _ { K = 1 } ^ { N } \left\{ - j w d _ { 3 1 } E _ { p } h _ { p c } w _ { 2 } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \sum _ { q = 1 } ^ { n } \eta _ { q } \left( w \right) \left[ w ^ { \prime } ( l _ { 2 } ) - w ^ { \prime } ( 0 ) \right] - j w \frac { \varepsilon _ { 3 3 } ^ { s } A } { h _ { p } } V _ { p } \left( w \right) \right\}
$$

Where $\eta _ { q }$ is the Fourier form of the $T _ { q }$ , and in this model, $n = 1 , 2 , 3 . \ V _ { p } ( w )$ is the Fourier form of $v ( t )$ , and $c _ { 0 }$ is the parasitic capacitance. Therefore the voltage $V _ { P } ( w )$ wcan be written as in Eq. (7).

$$
V _ { p } \left( w \right) = \sum _ { K = 1 } ^ { N } \frac { h _ { p } B } { j w \varepsilon _ { 3 3 } ^ { s } A + \left( 1 + j w c _ { 0 } + \frac { 1 } { R _ { L } } \right) h _ { p } }
$$

Where

$$
B = j w d _ { 3 1 } E _ { p } h _ { p c } w _ { 2 } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \sum _ { q = 1 } ^ { n } \eta _ { q } ( w ) \left[ w _ { q i } ^ { \prime } ( l _ { 2 } ) - w _ { q i } ^ { \prime } ( 0 ) \right]
$$

Eq. (7) represents the voltage generated by using bifurcate-shape piezoelectric energy harvesting structure. Hence, considering the load resistance $R _ { L }$ , the voltage across the resistive load is given as.

$$
V ( t ) = R _ { L } i \left( t \right) = R _ { L } \sum _ { K = 1 } ^ { N } \left[ \frac { d Q \left( t \right) } { d t } \right] = R _ { L } \sum _ { K = 1 } ^ { N } \left[ - d _ { 3 1 } E _ { p } h _ { p c } \int _ { 0 } ^ { w _ { 2 } } \int _ { 0 } ^ { l _ { 2 } } \frac { \partial ^ { 2 } y _ { r e l } } { \partial x ^ { 2 } } d x - \frac { \varepsilon _ { 3 3 } ^ { s } A } { h _ { p } } \dot { v } _ { p } \left( t \right) \right]
$$

sections.heading: A. Characteristics of the resonance frequency
sections.text:
The vibration cloud picture of the first four order modal simulation of the harvester is shown in Fig. 2. As shown in Fig. 2, the resonance frequencies from first order to fourth order are $2 9 2 . 1 1 \mathrm { H z }$ , 386.76Hz, 881.41Hz, and $1 0 2 1 . 3 0 \mathrm { H z }$ , respectively. For each sequence, a maximum displacement is appeared at the free end of the proof mass and the tendency of the maximum amplitude moves from both sides to the middle. The influence of distance between inside and outside cantilevers is shown in Table I. It can be seen that, although in some distance (distance ${ \mathrm { : = } } 3 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ ), resonance frequency has a significant reduction, with the increase of distance between the inside and outside cantilevers; it presents a trend of growth, in general. Within a certain range ( $1 0 \mu \mathrm { m } \sim 2 0 \mu \mathrm { m } )$ ), the change of frequency is very severe. It is interesting to note that the distance of the same side of the two cantilevers should be as close as possible. ![](images/ef532976da13d2ab9b95e4d9fb1e95a7220f8da28f0d9c2530e2d4c2130e32ba.jpg) FIG. 2. In order to perform the displacement condition of the device in resonant frequency and natural frequency, Fig. 3(a) and Fig. 3(b) shows the main view and the lateral view of the three directions(X axis, Y axis, Z axis) displacement summation of the first order(292.11Hz) harmonic simulation in $1 \mathrm { g }$ acceleration. It can be seen in simulation that the vice beam will have a bending deformation and the deformation of right side is larger than that from the left side, this will lead to a damage of the device in a large frequency, which is in agreement with the results from Fig. 2. Results on the influence between the resonance frequency and the displacement of cantilevers are shown in Fig. 3(c). It can be indicated that the largest displacement is produced at the resonance frequency, at the same time, with the increase of the resonant frequency, the displacement becomes larger and larger, and the displacement of the inside cantilever is greater than the outside cantilever at the third order $( 8 8 1 . 4 1 \mathrm { H z } )$ , which means the device has a huge deformation and exceeds the tolerance of the device. Fig. 3(d) shows the relationship between the displacement in different direction and the natural frequency, it can be seen that at the low frequency $( < 4 0 0 \mathrm { H z } )$ , the maximum displacement occurs at the direction of Z axis, which means the device work in normal state. However, when the frequency is over $4 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ , the direction of the $\mathrm { X }$ axis and Y axis is much higher than $\boldsymbol { \mathrm { Z } }$ axis, showing that the device produces a large deformation and tendency bend inwardly. It can be indicated that the device can not endure higher resonant frequency, and it should work in an appropriate frequency. ![](images/f8e196726d2ace63d67981ad5726db3341cf7b38f974e8803ff0a95452e80131.jpg) FIG. 3. The displacement condition of the device (a) in main view (b) in lateral view. The influence between the natural frequency with (c) the location of cantilevers (d) the displacement of different direction. ![](images/9c404887ee6e447afe1b576a26cfddb87e9972526793c7488b2b8b486659f040.jpg) FIG. 4. The cloud picture of the stress intensity from first order to fourth order of the device. For the entire device, the factor of stress intensity also cannot be ignored. The cloud picture of the stress intensity from the first order to the fourth of the device is shown in Fig. 4. As shown in Fig. 4, the stress intensity from main beam to vice beam is in general. Compared with main beam and vice beam, the stress intensity of the cantilever is negligible. In the resonant frequency of the second order, the stress intensity on the main beam become maximum, also when the resonant frequency is over $8 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ , the stress intensity is forced on the vice beam and both sides of the main beam, that means the device presents an arc-shape. It can be seen that the device should work in the suitable frequency range and in order to extend the lifetime of the device, the length-width ratio of the main beam and vice beam should be considered.

sections.heading: B. Characteristics of the voltage and power
sections.text:
Fig. 5(a) and Fig. 5(b) show the cloud picture of the open-circle voltage on first and second order of the device. From the previous analysis, because of the deformation of the piezoelectric wafer, the charge makes displacement, and resulting voltage. From the Fig. 5(a), the voltage presents a symmetrical form and Fig. 5(b) shows that the voltage from the left side is higher than right side of the device. It can be noted that in order to get the maximum efficiency of the voltage, the device must work in the appropriate range. ![](images/df94bc113c42dfead59f31329bcc902a09a6dcf6450cd1f45bd76bf83b33dd02.jpg) FIG. 5. The cloud picture of the open-circle voltage (a) on first order (b) on second order of the device. ![](images/023c502830e95ce1d812260c7bc1d61bd98c88fb1e8944c6a36eb40c36ba04ec.jpg) FIG. 6. The change of the open-circle voltage (a) with decreasing length of piezoelectric layer (b) on different location of cantilever. Fig. 6(a) plots the change of the open-circuit voltage with decreasing length of piezoelectric layer. The result shows that the open-circle voltage presents a downward trend in general, and a maximum value of $1 . 6 5 \mathrm { V }$ is obtained at the length of $1 9 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ . In terms of a single cantilever, the voltage increases along with increasing frequency below the resonance frequency, and there is a peak value at the resonance frequency. For instance, when the length of cantilever is $1 7 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , the maximum value is $1 . 2 5 \mathrm { V }$ (at $3 1 2 . 8 7 \mathrm { H z }$ ). Meanwhile, Fig. 6(b) shows the open-circle voltage gathered from the different location of cantilever. It indicates that the voltage obtained from outside cantilever is higher than the inside ones, and for the outside cantilever, the third order voltage is significantly less than the second one. This is because the device cannot able to bear the large frequency. Therefore, in order to ensure the maximum output performance of the device, this should work in a low frequency. Fig. 7(a) shows that the open-circle voltage obtained from the different thickness of piezoelectric layer under the acceleration of 1g. The range of thickness is $0 . 5 \mu \mathrm { m }$ to $8 . 5 \mu \mathrm { m }$ . As shown in Fig. 7(a), the voltage can reach to the maximum when the thickness is well matched to the best thickness ratio, at the same time, the open-circle voltage of inside cantilever increases gently because of the weak vibration which could be indicated from Figure 2. In the case of the different vibration condition, the relationship between the open-circle voltage and excited frequency under different accelerations is plotted in Fig. 7(b). It can be seen that the open-circle voltage amplitude is maximal varies with the amplitude of the excited acceleration and decrease with the increase of the acceleration amplitude in general. Therefore in order to obtain the maximum voltage, the device should be designed according to real application. ![](images/f4fbcf7219c17f98e96592293eede54f1ed5e02a3c053bbc90739c5e5a420065.jpg) FIG. 7. The open-circle voltage obtained from (a) the different thickness of the piezoelectric layer under the acceleration of $1 \mathrm { g }$ (b) the different acceleration. ![](images/07a8eae464e6829ed446dae9c336f1c742fb23dd70490e68a55f3ef52bec6c31.jpg) FIG. 8. The equivalent circuit diagram of the system. For the entire device, the quality of the output power is another important indicator.13–15 In this article, the equivalent circle of the system is used to measurement the output power of the device. Fig. 8 shows the equivalent circle of the system. The energy collecting part is equivalent to the ideal current source in parallel a capacitance $C _ { 0 }$ , through a rectifier bridge, $C _ { L }$ is a rectifier capacitance and the value with several orders of magnitude higher than $C _ { 0 }$ , $R _ { L }$ is a load resistance. Results on the output power of the energy harvester as a function of load resistance at inside and outside piezoelectric layer are presented in Fig. 9(a). In this experiment, the vibration frequency is resonant. The Fig. 9(a) shows that the output power obtained in outside piezoelectric layer is higher than inside ones in general, and for a single piezoelectric layer, the maximum value is obtained at the optimum load resistance. It is observed from outside one that the value of output power is below the maximum when the resistance around is the optimum resistance, and the maximum output power reaches $0 . 1 5 5 \mathrm { m W }$ at the optimum resistance of about $0 . 4 \mathbf { M } \Omega$ . Furthermore, Fig. 9(b) presents the output voltage and power as a function of acceleration levels under optimal resistance when the resonance frequency is used. As shown in Fig. 7(b), the output power and voltage are related to the acceleration level. The electrical output of the energy harvester increase with respect to an increase in acceleration. The maximum output voltage and power are 3V and $0 . 1 5 5 \mathrm { m W }$ at $1 \mathrm { g }$ acceleration level and resonance frequency of 292.11Hz. The output performance of the energy harvester in different working conditions, comparing with other published MEMS devices are listed in Table III. sections.heading: IV. CONCLUSION
sections.text: This paper presents a novel MEMS-based bifurcate-shape piezoelectric energy harvester. Through the improvement of basic equations, the theoretical analysis is conducted for the resonance frequency and electrical parameters under the first order. Then the experiment is conducted to demonstrate the effect of structure on performance, and the result shows that the harvester can reach a maximum open-circle voltage of $3 . 3 \mathrm { V }$ under an acceleration of $1 \mathrm { g }$ at $2 9 2 . 1 1 \mathrm { H z }$ of frequency, and the output power can reach $0 . 1 5 5 \mathrm { m W }$ in the optimum load resistance of 0.4MΩ. The power density is $4 9 6 . 7 9 \mu \mathrm { W } \mathrm { m m } ^ { - 3 }$ . The effectiveness of this device would be improved with further optimization in the design and structure parameters, such as more cantilevers on the vice-beam and a certain angle produced between the cantilever and the beam. The results show a good potential for low-power electronic devices.
